content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes using neural networks to predict source code complexity (Big-O runtime complexity). To do that they train against a dataset of 4120 Java codes which were annotated as to their complexity by human annotators. As existing Transformer architectures cannot always scale to long code lengths, they propose exploiting the hierarchical structure of code with a hierarchical Transformer. They split the code into classes and classes into methods. They then recursively apply the Transformer architecture at each level. Max pooling is used to condense method and class embeddings into a single embedding vector. For class embeddings, if the class contains the main method, they use the main method embedding as the class embedding instead of max pooling. They pretrain their models with multiple additional auxiliary objectives. They also do dead code elimination as a preprocessing step.

The model with pretraining and dead code elimination seems to be the best showing consistent improvements on both the random and problem level split over rival models. However on the problem level split (where it is ensured there's no problem overlap between train and test), the improvement is minor over PLBART (63.8 -> 64.8 accuracy) despite PLBART being a much simpler model.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The paper has several interesting ideas. It explores

(1) Hierarchical Transformers -- while this has been explored in the context of language in the past, they adapt it to code and do so in a novel manner
(2) Pretraining with code specific auxiliary objectives
(3) Dead code elimination preprocessing

Weaknesses:

(1) It's unclear to me whether the number of parameters in their model is the same as the number of parameters in other models. If their model has more parameters, this fact alone could explain the better performance given the known language model scaling laws. Similarly it's not clear to me whether the pretraining data for their model as well as the baseline models was the same or different. If their model was pretrained on more data, then that too would explain performance differences.

(2) Is the test data deduped against the pretraining data?

(3) However, the improvements in terms of accuracy seem minor and it's not very clear where they are coming from. For example, the hierarchical architecture is motivated as a way to deal with longer code. However baseline architectures that do not have that hierarchical structure can best it (without 2, 3) even for long codes (Table 4). Alternatives for how to organize the hierarchy are also not explored. Likewise there's multiple possible auxiliary objectives but only a single one of them is explored.

(4) The performance improvements due to 2, 3 over 1 are also a bit erratic -- for example in Table 2, for the random split, the performance actually declines with the addition of 2, 3 and it's not clear why. In particular if including dead code can be useful for random splits, why would it not be useful for problem splits?

(5) It's unclear whether the splits for Tables 1, 3, 4 are the random split or the problem split and why results for both are not given. If it's the random split, I would suggest adding in the results for the problem split as well as that's the harder task and more likely to test whether the model is actually understanding the code well enough to predict complexity (as opposed to just learning some problem specific tokens and matching them to the complexity).

(6) No error bars on the results are given either.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity:

Unclear what the splits for Table 1, 3, 4 are.

Quality:

Error bars are not given for any of the results

Novelty:

The ideas are somewhat novel.
content.summary_of_the_review:
Most importantly, I think they need to explicitly state the number of parameters in their and baseline models. They also need to specify the pretraining data for all models as well as what steps they took to make sure the pretraining data did not overlap with the test data.

While the ideas are novel, the improvements they obtain are small. In particular, on the problem level split (where it is ensured there's no problem overlap between train and test), the improvement is minor over PLBART (63.8 -> 64.8 accuracy) despite PLBART being a much simpler model. I think a much more thorough investigation of the the ideas is warranted.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
The paper proposes a NN model for predicting the complexities of the code.
The proposed model uses a hierarchical architecture and multi-level pertaining objectives that are representative of code hierarchy (class, method, token, etc.)
They further construct a novel dataset to annotate code complexity.
The results show they are better or comparable with SOTA.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength:

+ Curation of a good dataset for algorithmic complexity prediction.

+ I really like the hierarchical multi-objective pertaining proposed in the paper to capture code representation. Such embedding can be tried for other downstream  PL-related tasks as well.

+ The authors evaluated many popular SOTA. They perform better for code with a larger length.


Weakness:
- I think the authors should dive a bit deeper into the evaluation. Table 4 shows the proposed method performs better for the larger code base. This makes me wonder whether the code with a smaller size has enough methods and classes to show the effectiveness of the proposed method. I would recommend authors give some statistics on the number of methods and classes per sample.

- It is not clear why certain previous works (e.g., PLBART and AST-NN) are performing better for O(1) and O(n^3). 

- It is not clear whether the authors fine-tuned the SOTA (e.g., ASTNN, GraphCodeBert, PLBART, CodeT5). In the problem splitting, the different between PLBART and proposed method is closed. It is import to understand how previous pretrained models are used.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: - The paper's proposed model is novel. However, certain experimental setting is not clear (as mentioned above). The dataset is a nice contribution.
content.summary_of_the_review:
To me, the novel model design and data curation part are good. However, more clarification is needed in the empirical part. 
The task is also not super interesting to do with an ML model.

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper address the problem of deciding the computational complexity of a given program by deep learning models with a hierarchical Transformer architecture. To support the training and validation of the models, it builds a code dataset consisting of 4120 Java codes from a code competition platform. The experimental results on the dataset show the effectiveness of the proposed hierarchical Transformer architecture.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength

1. The hierarchical Transformer architecture is a nice addition even though the notion of hierarchical learning is very common see ''Hierarchical Recurrent Neural Networks for Long-Term Dependencies '' and ''Hierarchical Graph Representation Learning with Differentiable Pooling''

Weakness

1.My main is that the motivation of the paper is weak. Regarding the third paragraph of the Introduction section, it is unclear why the authors say "**If AI can really understands programs as human programmers do and possibly replace them in future, then it is natural that AI can also understand how to write ‘algorithmically efficient’ programs rather than just memorize the code patterns seen from the training dataset.**". It is almost guaranteed that if a AI system can write correct programs more often than humans do, then most (if not all) would not worry if the AI system can not correctly predict the run-time complexity of algorithms and simply memorize code patterns from the training set. At this point, it's a consensus that state-of-the-art deep models memorize [1], however, are people stop using deep models just because they memorize? Authors' argument regarding the educational purpose is even weaker. The efficiency of code, especially written by novice programming learners, can be easily evaluated by test cases from online judge systems. Considering that formal methods exist which can analyzes the complexity of algorithms in a principled manner (i.e., with guarantees), authors need to do a much better job in justifying the complexity prediction task.

[1] Understanding deep learning requires rethinking generalization

2. The detailed design of the proposed method is unclear and not convincing. First, giving an intuition for formula 1 might be easier for readers to understand the class-level pre-training and its design choice. Second, it would be clear to have more discussion about the design of the hierarchical structure.  For example, the authors claim that the order of class or method declarations in a code does not affect its semantics, but it is not convincing when class A inherits class B.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think the paper has good experimental results and that the incorporation of the hierarchical architecture is useful.  While the novelty is not significant and there is not a thorough discussion about the design of the proposed method.

content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper studies the problem of code complexity prediction. It first proposes a new dataset consisted of java code sourced from the Codeforce portal and annotated with groundtruth complexity. This dataset is larger than existing dataset for code complexity prediction and  covers questions from more complexity classes.

There are two major challenges in this datasets. First, code context is usually longer than the pretrained context window of existing models. Second, there is only a small amount of training data available. For both challenges, this submission attempts to offer a solution. First, it proposes a new hierarchical transformer architecture that encodes java code on multiple levels. Second, it proposes a set of pretraining objectives, such as predicting the nested loop level. 

The proposed methods leads to new SOTA results when combined with the CodeBERT model, although the improvement is not ground-breaking. I have a few concerns about the empirical experiment setup, mainly around ablations and comparison with baseline (detailed below). My current recommendation is a weak accept and is willing to increase the rating if my concerns can be addressed in the author response period.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strength
1. The paper provides a new dataset, which is resourceful for future research
2. The proposed architecture and pretraining objectives are novel
3. The empirical comparison with prior methods favors the proposed method

## Weakness
### Concerns about the empirical results that the authors should addressed on author response
1. Based on Table 4, the advantage of the proposed method mostly comes from its stronger ability in dealing with longer code context. Can the author apply dead code elimination to the baseline methods as well? It seems that PLBART is pretty strong and applying dead code elimination can probably make it even stronger.
2. I expect a more detailed ablation study of the decisions made for the Hierarchical Attention module. 
2.1 The authors propose to use sset attention to handle the permutation invariance in java code. Is this design choice necessary and helpful? Can the authors show that using a normal transformer is worse?
2.2 How important is the proposed max pooling technique? Is there a possible unifying appraoch to handle methods that don't have a main method?

### Suggestions that could improve the empirical results but not necessary to include in the response period
1. As I understand, the pretraining objectives are architecture-agnostic and can be applied to other baseline models as well. Can the authors show this is helpful?

### Comments that the author can discuss in the response period but I don't expect new results
1. Code complexity prediction should be a general problem for differnet programming languages. However, both the dataset and the proposed methods are very java-specific.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
- The writing is clear.
- The proposed methods are novel and the proposed dataset is resourceful
- I believe the paper is reproducible.
content.summary_of_the_review: Good resource and novel methods. I have two specific requests on the empirical section that I expect the authors to fix during the response period. I am leaning toward accept the paper but gives a weak accept for now.

content.title: Deep Learning-based Source Code Complexity Prediction
content.TL;DR: We suggest a deep-learning based approach for estimating computational (time) complexity of given programs and provide the largest code complexity dataset as the benchmark.
content.abstract:
Deciding the computational complexity of algorithms is a really challenging problem even for human algorithm experts. Theoretically, the problem of deciding the computational complexity of a given program is undecidable due to the famous Halting problem. In this paper, we tackle the problem by designing a neural network that comprehends the algorithmic nature of codes and estimates the worst-case complexity.
First, we construct a code dataset called the CodeComplex that consists of 4,120Java codes submitted to programming competitions by human programmers and their complexity labels annotated by a group of algorithm experts. As far as we are aware, the CodeComplex dataset is by far the largest code dataset for the complexity prediction problem. Then, we present several baseline algorithms using the previous code understanding neural models such as CodeBERT, GraphCodeBERT, PLBART, and CodeT5. As the previous code understanding models do not work well on longer codes due to the code length limit, we propose the hierarchical Transformer architecture which takes method-level code snippets instead of whole codes and combines the method-level embeddings to the class-level embedding and ultimately to the code-level embedding. Moreover, we introduce pre-training objectives for the proposed model to induce the model to learn both the intrinsic property of the method-level codes and the relationship between the components.
Lastly, we demonstrate that the proposed hierarchical architecture and pre-training objectives achieve state-of-the-art performance in terms of complexity prediction accuracy compared to the previous code understanding models.
